children: Fast-fashion giant Shein slid in its long-awaited trading debut, as regulatory headwinds and slowing sales challenge a company once valued at US$100 billion.

The retailer's stock tumbled as much as 10% in early trading in Hong Kong. Shein's shares fell as low as 43.72 Hong Kong dollars on Tuesday before regaining some ground to trade at HK$44.50, implying a market capitalization of around US$24 billion.

The listing by the China-founded company famous for ultracheap, trendy apparel has been years in the making. A series of regulatory obstacles, heightened by geopolitical tensions, have hurt Shein's business and complicated efforts to go public.

Shein's circuitous path toward an IPO included attempts to list in New York and London, both of which fell through. But even with the cut-down valuation, the IPO is still one of the largest in Hong Kong so far this year, behind tech names such as Nvidia supplier Zhongji Innolight and Apple supplier Luxshare Precision Industry.
Shein's offering drew cornerstone investors including General Atlantic and Greenwoods Asset Management Hong Kong. These shares face a lock-up period until the end of February.
Existing shareholders hold about 90% of Shein's shares. Some shareholders face a longer lock-up period until the end of August 2028.

"March is the genuine test, when ... far more stock becomes tradable. Between now and then, Shein needs to prove there's an engine room worth paying for behind the label," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia Pacific at etoro.
On Monday, Shein set its final offer price at HK$48.56, raising HK$13.60 billion, equivalent to US$1.73 billion.
The stock was last down 8.5%, underperforming the Hang Seng Tech Index's 0.7% drop.

Shein, a key competitor of PDD Holdings' Temu, started selling its products in the U.S. around 2012 and gained popularity during the pandemic when more people shopped online. Its major supply chain is in China's southern manufacturing hub of Guangdong, where most of its contract manufacturers are based.

"We think the decline in market perception of Shein reflects slower revenue growth amid a slew of geopolitical challenges as well as increased competition," said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research in Asia at Morningstar, before the listing.

"While sales in Asia are helping to offset a fall in U.S. revenue, we're probably looking at a period of single-digit revenue growth for the company and this maturing outlook is likely to limit investor excitement," she said.
Market attention has also shifted from traditional e-commerce companies to the AI and robotics sectors, where investors are more willing to pay a premium for potential.

Shein's listing this week allowed it to avoid paying out billions to early investors. If Shein hadn't sold shares by the end of the year, the company would have been required to pay out nearly $4.4 billion in cash to holders of its convertible redeemable preferred shares.
